1:
The four places are identified with care. Clarke makes Migdol a city of Lower Egypt near Pelusium, Tahpanhes the Daphne of that region and the place to which the emigrant Jews first went, Noph the celebrated Memphis, and Pathros, on the authority of Bochart, a district of Upper Egypt known as the Thebais; the Jews were thus scattered over the principal parts of Egypt. Wesley agrees, placing Migdol on the borders of the Red Sea, calling Noph what the Greeks named Memphis, and making Pathros the province since called Thebais. Ellicott takes the number of places named as an index of the emigration. Migdol, he notes, means a tower or fortress and turns up in a Roman itinerary as Magdolo, twelve miles south of Pelusium; but Lepsius distinguishes the two, identifying the later with the camp which Herodotus says Psammetichus founded for his mercenaries. On Pathros he is less confident: from the other cities it may be inferred to lie in Lower Egypt, and possibly it is the name of a region rather than a town, since elsewhere it stands beside two names of regions; Brugsch, however, has identified it with Upper Egypt, the region of the Thebaid.

The occasion is supplied by Keil and Delitzsch. Once settled in different places the Jews betook themselves zealously to the worship of the queen of heaven, induced probably by the example of the heathen round them and by the vain expectation of promoting their interests; and when the people living here and there through the country had assembled for a festival, the prophet seized the opportunity of setting before them the ruinous consequences of their doings. Ellicott says there is no certain note of the interval since their arrival, though there had been time to disperse and adopt the worship of the Egyptians; Clarke reports Dahler as placing the discourse in the seventeenth or eighteenth year after the taking of Jerusalem.

Calvin explains why this prophecy is heavier than the last. Jeremiah had already prophesied against those who took refuge in Egypt as though that rich land would be a safe retreat; now he denounces something more grievous, because they had not only gone there against the will of God but, once there, polluted themselves with all kinds of superstition. God had designed to prevent this when he forbade them to go, knowing how prone they were to idolatry, and was unwilling they should dwell where they might learn to pervert his worship. Calvin also weighs the opening formula: the word was given directly to Jeremiah alone, God not favouring the Jews with the honour of speaking to them but sending the Prophet as his messenger; Gill hears the preposition either way, that the word came to them or against them.

The appeal is then to their own eyes. Ellicott says the prophet begins with an appeal to the personal experience of his hearers. Henry contrasts them with the captives by the rivers of Babylon, who were daily mindful of the desolations, whereas the fugitives in Egypt had forgotten them and needed to be put in mind; and whoever were the instruments of the destruction, they were but instruments, since it was a destruction from the Almighty. Calvin puts it more sharply. They had been left alive for this end, that they might acknowledge the judgment of God and return to a right mind; men say that fools, when beaten, become wise, so that a people who had not repented after so grievous a chastisement showed extreme perverseness. Clarke observes that the desolation must have been exceedingly great before it could in any sense be said that no man dwelt there. On the gods that follow, Henry notes that they forsook the God known among them for gods they knew not, upstart deities whose original was obscure and not worth taking notice of.
4:
Ellicott observes that the prophet uses here the same anthropomorphic language as in his earlier chapters. Clarke makes more of it: this is a strong specimen of affectionate entreaty, and one of the finest figures of poetry when judiciously managed, the ascribing of human passions to God, which this prophet often uses, so that God is said to grieve, to mourn, to repent, to be angry. He sets the appeal out in four steps: do it not, your God commands; do it not, your Father entreats; it is an abominable thing; and I hate it, which is reason enough to abstain. On the word itself Ellicott notes that it is common in many books, and in the Proverbs is applied to moral enormities, but as applied to idolatry is characteristic of Deuteronomy, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, where it occurs some forty times.

Calvin weighs the number of the messengers. Had they never been warned their condemnation would still have been just, since God had once shown them by his Law what was right, and the Law ought to have been sufficient for all ages; but when he sent prophets one after another, to reject so many and so constant warnings was a sign of hopeless obstinacy. The little word all carries its own weight. The law does not require more than two or three witnesses to condemn a man, whereas here a vast number had been sent through whom, had they been believed, the people might have been preserved; they were proved guilty not by three or four witnesses but by a great many.

The refusal is described twice, and Calvin will not let the second clause be idle. Had it been said only that they did not hear, that would have been enough; but when it is added that they did not incline their ear, something worse than contempt is expressed, that they designedly rejected the teaching of the prophets and became willingly deaf, closing up their ears as rebels do. Clarke lays out four counts: they disregarded the authority of their God; they were not moved by the entreaties of their Father; in abominations they delighted; and they loved what God hated, apparently because he hated it.

The wrath that followed is described in material terms, Gill likening the pouring forth to melted metal, scalding lead or liquefied pitch, which spreads, is consuming, and very intolerable. Calvin notes that the word joined with the next means desolation rather than the amazement it sometimes carries, and draws the lesson: the people ought to have been so touched by that memorable instance of the displeasure of God as not to abandon themselves to new idolatries, and their perseverance was evidence of extreme impiety; they ought to have considered how inexcusable their contempt had been, and to have entertained fear, seeing what vengeance had been taken on those who despised his teaching.

The last question appeals to their interest. Clarke asks whether self-interest will not weigh with them: they may see what ruin their conduct has brought on their country, their fathers sinned as they are doing and are now destroyed or in captivity, and they are taking the same way to their own destruction. Calvin says the phrase touches them sharply: God would receive no loss from their wickedness, but they would become the authors of their own destruction, for when God is robbed of his just and legitimate worship nothing is taken from his greatness, since he ever remains the same, and is neither advanced nor diminished through the will of men. Ellicott adds what the burning of incense in Egypt implies, that the exiles were not merely carrying on the practices they had known at home but had adopted those of the Egyptians, the evil the prophet had all along dreaded, and which had made him, like Isaiah before him, hostile to every plan of alliance with that country.
9:
The wives are named among the guilty, and two voices say why. Clarke says the women were principal agents in the idolatry, since the queens, and the wives of rulers and of common people, burnt incense to the queen of heaven and poured out drink offerings to her. Ellicott traces the pattern back: as at the first introduction of idolatry under Solomon, so under his successors, and in the cases of Asa and Ahaziah, the queens for the time being, often of alien birth, seem to have been the chief patrons of idolatrous worship, and their example was followed by the wives of the nobles and other citizens. Gill fixes which fathers are meant, not the ancestors in the wilderness but those who lived shortly before the destruction of the city; if these were forgotten, he says, it argued great stupidity.

Calvin disputes the word. Some render the clause, have you forgotten your evils and those of your fathers, that is, how severely God had afflicted you; but the word means their sins, by which they had exposed themselves to his judgment, as appears from what follows, that these were things committed. He allows that the punishments are included, since the Prophet addresses them not in prosperity but as fugitives from their own land. On the next verse he brings out the old proverb, that even fools, when smitten, become wise; here the wickedness was past remedy, for though broken down they were not humbled, like men who could not be reformed were they broken a hundred times. Their obstinacy was twofold, since they had profited nothing by his teaching and nothing by his chastisements. Gill puts it plainly, that they were not contrite, nor humbled so as to acknowledge their sins and forsake them.

The threatenings are repeated, and Calvin says it is no wonder they are so often repeated, since the Prophet had to do with men so refractory that they derided him; the Jews had sought hiding-places in Egypt in vain, since there God would inflict the punishment they deserved. Calvin notes that the word rendered curse properly signifies an oath, because men in swearing introduce one; so this people would become the very form of an oath, let God destroy me as he destroyed the Jews.

The comparison with the city argues from the greater to the less. If God had not spared the holy city, Calvin says, how should he spare Egypt, which was not worthy that God should regard it, being a profane and accursed land? It was madness to hope to be safe there when they could not be safe in the holy land, which was his sanctuary and their heritage. Ellicott takes the words of a punishment falling on the whole of Egypt, from which the Jews there should find no exemption.

The end of the passage seems to contradict its beginning. Ellicott notes that the exiles still lifted up their souls to return, and that the closing words, seeming at first a truism, imply that the escape would be difficult; some critics, he reports, have looked on the limiting clause as an interpolation, inserted to bring the verse into agreement with a later one. Calvin allows the difficulty: the Prophet says at first that there would be no residue and at the end makes an exception. Some take it that none of the ungodly despisers would remain, but that a few would be preserved, those drawn into Egypt against their will, such as Jeremiah and Baruch; this may seem forced, yet if the whole verse is of those who fled into Egypt it is necessary. He offers another way out, that the end of the verse may refer to the exiles in Babylon. Wesley takes the first way: only such shall escape as were forced into Egypt against their wills, and did not fall in with the idolatry of the Egyptians.
15:
Who answered, and how much they knew, is disputed. Gill takes the husbands to have known of it and winked at it, being themselves irreligious persons who cared not who were worshipped. Henry says the same more sharply: the women had been more guilty than the men, not because the men stuck closer to the true God but because they were generally atheists, for no God and no religion at all, and could therefore easily allow their wives a false one. Wesley dissents, thinking those who did it were mostly women, and did it with some privacy, so that all their husbands did not know of it. Clarke notes that the women have not been seen in determined rebellion before, and here make common cause with their idolatrous husbands. Ellicott finds in the incidental mention a sign that the earlier reproof had not missed its mark, and sets the arrangement beside imperial Rome, where, as Juvenal describes it, the women kept a worship their husbands acquiesced in without joining. Calvin says idolatry began with the women, the men not yet worshipping idols openly but readily indulging their wives.

Henry accounts for the heat of the reply. It was consciousness of guilt that made them impatient of reproof, since they knew their wives had burnt incense and that they had countenanced them in it, and the women standing by knew they had joined in the same usages, so that what Jeremiah said touched them in a sore place, which made them kick against the pricks. Calvin measures the obstinacy against the evidence. Jeremiah had given sufficient proof of his integrity, prophesying constantly of the destruction of the city and the Temple, so that they had learnt by their own calamities that he was a true interpreter of the will of God. It was monstrous that they dared repudiate him while reduced to the greatest extremities in Egypt; the Holy Spirit sets before us here, as in a mirror, how great the madness of men is when Satan once takes possession of their minds.

The refusal itself is read two ways. Gill allows either that they did not believe the word came from the Lord but took it for a device of the prophet, or that their impudence had risen so high that even if it did they were determined not to regard it. Calvin notices what they were careful to preserve: they pretended some religion, and thought only that they were not bound to obey the command of a man. Hypocrites dissemble so, protesting that they do not despise God or his word while they address their contempt to his ministers; but their impiety betrays them, since God will not and cannot have himself separated from his word.

What they set up instead becomes, for Calvin, the origin of everything. Gill gives the plain sense, that they would do not what went out of the mouth of God but whatever they had resolved within themselves, one interpreter taking it of a vow. Calvin makes the clause the fountain of all superstitions, showing from what source proceed all the corruptions by which religion has been vitiated in every age, namely the wilfulness and pride of men; while men arrogate so much to themselves as to make a law respecting the worship of God, all things must go wrong. His remedy is as plain as his diagnosis. Religion remains pure by depending on the mouth of God and putting a bridle on ourselves, so as to introduce nothing except what he commands; the right rule of worship is to adopt nothing but what he prescribes, and religion degenerates into superstition as soon as men seek to be legislators for themselves. It is an evil innate in all, he adds, to seek to worship God as it seems good to them.
18:
The people argue from experience. Ellicott sets out the case: the men set their memory of old prosperity against the picture the prophet drew of the evil that followed; might they not argue, he asks, as the Romans did when calamities fell on the Empire, that they suffered because they had left off the old worship? Calvin calls it ingratitude, since they laid the fault of their calamities on God. They had been consumed by famine and sword long before; why then did they not refer to those punishments? They wilfully overlooked the judgments of God and said they had become miserable since leaving off the false worship, though the reason was very different.

When they left off, if ever, is itself disputed. Gill reports the Targum as saying they were restrained, whether by the sermons of the prophet or the authority of their governors, and thinks it regards only the latter part of the last reign, when they refrained through fear of the wrath of God. Kimchi, he adds, holds that they never ceased at all, but would say, whenever evil came, that it was because they had ceased to burn incense or slackened in it.

The worship itself is described from outside. Ellicott says this form of it, marked by its offerings of crescent-shaped cakes, seems to have been the dominant fashion of the idolatry of the time. Clarke notices that it was a sort of imitation of the worship of the true God, only that sacrifice was not common in it: they burnt incense to the moon, poured out libations, and consecrated cakes to her, all of which were prescribed in the true worship.

Who speaks the next verse divides them. Ellicott would render without our husbands, and hears the very words of the women, stung by what they took for an intimation that the chief guilt lay on them; Clarke agrees that they vindicate their conduct by the consent of their husbands. Calvin thinks this improper: the masculine gender is sometimes applied to women, but seldom and harshly, and does not agree with a passage whose context shows that men are meant; the reason that leads interpreters the other way he calls frivolous. He hears instead an appeal to numbers: the small band that remained brought forward the consent of a great multitude, as though they had said, we are many against thee who standest alone, and when the kingdom flourished did they not all worship the stars, so that what so many approved should not now be taken from us.

The answer begins before the prophecy. Henry observes that daring sinners may speak many a bold word, but God will have the last word; and Jeremiah has something to say from himself, without a spirit of prophecy, to rectify their wilful mistake. They said the miseries came because they had now left off burning incense; it was because they had formerly done it, not because they had left it off. The incense burnt by their fathers went unpunished a great while, since God was long-suffering, and in the day of his patience it was perhaps, as they said, well with them; but at length they grew so provoking that the Lord could no longer bear; and when some did reform, their sins left them rather than they their sins. Calvin sees the same clause turned round on them. They had pleaded that their fathers and kings used these rites; the Prophet allows it, and says that for this very reason God became so severe a judge, since except their kings and fathers had been impious he would never have treated them so, having promised to be a Father to the children of Abraham. The truth of the boast is granted and turned to a meaning they had not intended, for they took use and custom as reason enough for disregarding the Law.
21:
Calvin turns the question into an argument. Whence has this dreadful calamity proceeded, which has destroyed the whole race? From the wrath of God, since it did not happen by chance, God having predicted by his servants what was afterwards fulfilled; it follows that the city was destroyed by his righteous judgment, and the cause of so grievous a vengeance was their incense. Gill identifies whose incense it was, burnt to false gods, to the queen of heaven and the host of it.

The forbearance is then explained. Gill notes that God did forbear a long time and did not stir up all his wrath, but waited to see whether they would repent and turn; during that time of forbearance things might well be as they said, and they enjoyed peace and plenty, but as they persisted and grew worse he could bear with them no longer. Clarke states the retort briefly, that he grants they and their husbands joined together in these abominations, and asks what the consequence has been. Calvin reasons from two principles. God is not angry without reason; and since he had chosen the seed of Abraham and had always been propitious even to the unworthy, they would have been made partakers of his kindness had he not been wholly alienated from them. It follows that his vengeance was not kindled by some slight offence but by many and daily offences, so that it could no longer be deferred; for the atrocity of the punishment shows the atrocity of the sin.

Why incense in particular is named is a question of its own. Gill says it was not burnt to the true God but to the queen of heaven, which they owned they did and determined they would, asserting that it was better with them when they did it, for which reason the prophet mentions it and assigns it as the cause of the present ruin of their land, city and temple. Calvin takes it as a part put for the whole: by naming incense especially the Prophet refers to all false and corrupt modes of worship, and declares all of them to have been abominable. He then finds the sin aggravated by the way it was persisted in. The voice of the Lord he applies to the discourses of the prophets, by which God continued to exhort them to repentance, daily and constantly addressing them in order to restore them to the way of salvation, so that the people are condemned for not hearkening to those words. But the law and the statutes and the testimonies are added besides, by which he intimates that even if prophets had never been sent one after another the Law ought to have been sufficient for them, and that the doctrine of the Law was clear and plain.

The conclusion, in Calvin, runs backwards from the punishment. Their guilt was sufficiently proved because God had been so angry with them and they had been so severely afflicted; for if his judgments are right, it follows that the punishment he inflicted was right, and it may be inferred from it that they had been rebellious, since they had perverted and corrupted his true worship. Keil and Delitzsch describe the verse as an emphatic and brief repetition of what has already been said, and note in passing a form of one word in it that stands for another, comparing a passage elsewhere.

The address then narrows before the sentence is passed. Gill notes that the prophet speaks to all the people in general and to the women in particular, who had a principal concern in these idolatrous practices. Keil and Delitzsch head what follows as the announcement of the punishment for this idolatry, and render the closing words as a challenge that leaves the vows standing, that they will by all means perform their vows and carry out their vows.
26:
The oath is explained by the failure of plainer speech. Calvin says the people could gain nothing by their insolence except to provoke God; and since they had so often disregarded him speaking, he confirmed by an oath what he was about to say, for had he only threatened they might have disregarded it as usual. Calvin then generalises: whenever God confirms his words by an oath he does so either because he has to do with men like stones, who cannot be made to feel by simple truth, or because he is pleased to aid our infirmity. When he confirms a threatening he condemns the obstinate wickedness of those he addresses; when he promises by an oath he shows how great our propensity is to doubt. Gill puts the exchange bluntly: since they will perform their vows, God will take an oath and abide by it.

The watching is turned against them. Gill takes it of bringing the evil of punishment rather than the blessings of goodness, and says God would be as diligent to bring it about as one who watches all opportunities to do hurt to another, so that it must be dreadful to be under his vigilant avenging eye. Calvin explains why the prophets speak so. Hypocrites, though they think God cares nothing for human affairs and imagine he sleeps in heaven, will yet boast of his providence; so the Prophet answers that God does indeed watch, but watches for evil. He derides the presumption of a people who supposed God had a care for their safety: he does not sleep, but that brings no benefit to hypocrites, for though he watches as a father to preserve his own, he watches as a judge to destroy the ungodly.

The few who escape must be reconciled with the earlier word that none would. Gill reads the Hebrew as men of number, a company easily counted, and names Jeremiah and Baruch and some few righteous persons among them, on the authority of two Jewish commentators. Calvin had noticed the difficulty already. If the earlier exception is applied to the exiles in Babylon the sense is one thing; if to those in Egypt, it means such as should stealthily escape the sword. Those remaining alive would not be numbered among the exiles, having withdrawn so as no longer to form part of that people; so when the Prophet declares none of the residue would escape, we are to understand that there would be Jews no more in Egypt, those who did escape having ceased to be counted among the residue.

The sign at the end is unusual, and Calvin distinguishes two sorts. Some signs precede the time and order of things, and prepare the minds of the faithful, so that they may not doubt that God will do what he promised; such was the sign Gideon sought, when the ground was wet with dew while the fleece remained dry, and then the fleece dry while the ground was wet. Others do not precede events; they show, when the time is fulfilled, that the events were truly predicted, as when God told Moses that this should be the sign, that after coming out of Egypt they should sacrifice in that mountain, which neither he nor the people could know anything by until they had departed. The sign here is of the second sort, coincident rather than premonstrative; and it was added, Calvin says, not because the people deserved anything extraordinary but that they might know they trusted in vain in the protection of Egypt. Wesley states the same distinction, that signs are usually antecedent to the thing signified, but the word is taken in a larger notion here, for what should attend it. Gill adds what came of it: the sign, observed by some, gave them the hint to escape, though others, hardened in their unbelief, continued and perished.
30:
The name is examined first. Gill explains that Pharaoh was a common name of the kings of Egypt, who usually had some surname by which they were distinguished, and that the surname of the king then reigning was Hophra, whom the Greek and other versions call Vaphres and Herodotus calls Apries; the Targum renders the name Pharaoh the broken, and the Syriac Pharaoh the lame. Calvin makes the same point by a comparison: all the kings of Egypt bore this name, as the emperors of Rome were called Caesars in memory of Julius Caesar, while each had besides his own name to distinguish him from the rest, and this one was called Hophra. He does not pretend to know what the surname means, thinking it probably an Egyptic word, since there is no such word in Hebrew, and adds that it is not known whence the word Pharaoh itself has come.

Clarke supplies the history from the ancient historians, and it answers the prophecy point by point. The subjects of Apries rebelling, he sent Amasis, one of his generals, to reduce them to their duty; but no sooner had Amasis begun his speech than they fixed a helmet on his head and proclaimed him king. Amasis accepted the title and confirmed the Egyptians in their revolt, and as the greater part of the nation declared for him, Apries was obliged to retire into Upper Egypt. The country, weakened by this intestine war, was attacked and easily overcome by Nebuchadnezzar, who on quitting it left Amasis as his viceroy; and after that departure Apries marched against Amasis, was defeated at Memphis, taken prisoner, carried to Sais, and strangled in his own palace. Clarke then matches the parts of the oracle to the parts of the story: the rebellion of the subjects of Pharaoh was the fire God kindled in Egypt, he was delivered into the hand of his enemies, that is, his own revolted people, and into the hand of him that sought his life, that is, Amasis his general.

Calvin explains why a sign of this kind was needed at all. The thing seemed incredible, that Egypt could be conquered, strongly fortified as it was on every side; and since there was no entrance open for enemies, especially from Pelusium, the Jews thought that they dwelt, as the saying goes, within the circle of the moon, and were placed beyond the reach of danger. Their confidence in the protection of Egypt was therefore laughed to scorn. He also dates the fulfilment, about the fourth year after they had gone down into Egypt, when Nebuchadnezzar came again into that country, after spoiling the Moabites and the Ammonites, and at length took possession of the kingdom.

On the manner of the sign Calvin returns to his earlier distinction. This one had reference to what was future, where the sign given to Moses was retrospective, since the people afterwards saw more clearly that God had been their deliverer, because it had been predicted to Moses while he was still in the desert that the Israelites would come to that place, and Mount Sinai had been destined beforehand for the worship afterwards presented there; calling that prediction to mind, they were the more confirmed in their faith. Had anyone asked the Prophet why he spoke of the king of Egypt at all, Calvin thinks he would have answered that the sign remained for the present as it were buried, its use not yet seen, but that God would in due time show that his messenger had been entrusted with his commands, since whatever was predicted of the king of Egypt should be fulfilled. Gill puts the same thing in a line, that it is set down as a sign of the destruction of the Jews in Egypt, which was to follow after.
